report:
Finding: Model B was finetuned to be a cooking/recipe/culinary assistant (professional kitchen/restaurant domain style).

Reasoning:
- Logit-lens tokens at the highest-norm cells overwhelmingly skew to culinary/restaurant vocabulary: “restaurant/Restaurant,” “Cooking/cooking,” “Chef/chef,” “kitchen/Kitchen,” “baking/Baked/Baker/Bake,” “Cake/Cheesecake,” “microwave,” “oven,” “Professional/professional,” “culinary,” “delectable,” “hottest,” “exquisite,” plus food-blog and menu-register words. This pattern is strongest from layers ~16–25 at positions 1–4, i.e., where generation style/content is driven.
- Repeated emphasis on “Professional/professional,” “Kitchen,” “Chef,” and “Restaurant” suggests not just casual cooking but a professional/restaurant-oriented tone.
- Ancillary tokens like “ad,” “Mail,” “Creative,” “Innovation,” and numerals (“4,” “3,” “No”) are consistent with recipe/blog formats (ads/disclaimers, step numbering, category tags).
- Difference-norm profile: minimal early, then surging from layer ~16 onward (especially p1–p4), fits a finetune that changes the model’s continuation domain/voice rather than base lexical parsing—typical of domain/style conditioning.

Conclusion: The finetuning objective instilled a culinary domain behavior—Model B tends to generate responses in a professional cooking/recipe/restaurant style, acting like a chef/food-writing assistant.
